Research Themes

My work moves between classical gauge theory, the topology of field configurations, the geometry of noncommutative spaces, and algebraic approaches to quantum gravity and unification. A common thread is the use of deep symmetry arguments and mathematical structures to extract exact, illuminating results in regimes where brute-force methods fail.

Gauge Fields on Curved & Symmetric Spacetimes

A central thread running through much of my work is the question of what Yang–Mills gauge theory—the mathematical backbone of the Standard Model—looks like when transplanted onto the curved, cosmologically relevant spacetimes that general relativity demands. The challenge is both technical and conceptual: the high symmetry of spaces like de Sitter, anti-de Sitter, or Minkowski can be exploited systematically through the technique of equivariant dimensional reduction, which reduces the Yang–Mills equations to tractable ordinary differential equations whose solutions can often be written in closed form.

My PhD work, and several subsequent papers, pursued this programme across a range of backgrounds. On four-dimensional de Sitter space, we obtained a complete family of analytic SU(2) Yang–Mills solutions by exploiting its foliation structure and the isomorphism of the resulting symmetric spaces with Lorentz-group cosets—the field equations reducing elegantly to Newton's problem in an inverted double-well potential, with solutions given by Jacobi elliptic functions. Extending this to Minkowski space via non-compact coset spaces required a different approach, using SO(1,3)-invariant gauge fields in the temporal gauge to obtain new analytic solutions. The anti-de Sitter case, pursued during my postdoc in Hannover and presented in Prague and Vienna, reveals yet another rich family of exact gauge fields tied to the AdS isometry group. On the cosmological front, we analysed the stability of a coupled Einstein–Yang–Mills–Higgs system proposed as a model for the early universe, using Floquet analysis to show that all perturbative eigenmodes—classified by su(2) spin—are unstable, a result with implications for the viability of such cosmological scenarios.

Topology, Knots, and the Geometry of Light

One of the more striking facts in classical electromagnetism is that Maxwell’s equations—linear, well-understood, over a century old—admit solutions whose field lines form non-trivial closed knots: loops interlocked like links in a chain, field lines winding around each other in topologically protected configurations. The existence of such electromagnetic knots is not a curiosity but a consequence of deep conformal geometry: the conformal equivalence of de Sitter space with a compact cylinder over the three-sphere `S^3`, which in turn maps conformally to Minkowski space, provides a powerful machine for generating exact, finite-energy, finite-action knot solutions classified by the harmonics of `S^3`.

My work in this area, in collaboration with Olaf Lechtenfeld and others at ITP Hannover, has probed these structures from multiple angles. In one paper we established a complete “knot basis” of finite-action Maxwell fields labelled by spin `j`, derived a linear relation between energy and helicity, characterised the null-field subspace, and tracked electromagnetic flux across the Penrose diagram. In a follow-up we computed all fifteen conserved Noether charges associated with the conformal group for arbitrary complex linear combinations of knot-basis solutions at fixed spin, finding that scalar charges either vanish or are proportional to the energy—a remarkably clean geometric result. The physical reach of these configurations was then explored by numerically tracking the trajectories of charged test particles in knotted EM backgrounds, revealing intricate and sensitive dynamics. That some of these knot configurations have now been experimentally realized in the laboratory using laser beams with knotted polarization singularities makes this entire line of work feel less like pure mathematics and more like a glimpse of something genuinely fundamental about the structure of light.

Quantum Geometry of Noncommutative Spaces

The idea that spacetime might cease to be a smooth continuum at the Planck scale—replaced instead by something irreducibly discrete, “fuzzy,” governed by noncommutative coordinate algebras analogous to the phase-space uncertainty of quantum mechanics—has inspired a rich programme of research since the 1990s. The mathematical framework for studying the geometry of such spaces was pioneered by Fields medallist Alain Connes: a spectral triple, consisting of a (possibly non-commutative) algebra, a Hilbert space, and a Dirac operator, encodes enough geometric data to define a notion of distance between “points”—now understood as states of the algebra rather than locations in a manifold.

My early research, in collaboration with Biswajit Chakraborty at the S.N. Bose National Centre, Kolkata, contributed to this programme by developing a Hilbert–Schmidt operatorial formalism for computing spectral distances on the Moyal plane and the fuzzy sphere—models of noncommutative space that are both mathematically tractable and physically motivated. Our approach, which avoids the ambiguities inherent in star-product methods, allowed us to revise previous calculations and obtain new general results for arbitrary spin-`j` representations. In the doubled Moyal plane, we reproduced the Pythagorean equality between different sets of pure states and demonstrated the emergence of a Higgs-like field from fluctuations of the Dirac operator—a striking indication that the scalar boson responsible for mass generation may have a geometric origin in noncommutative structure. My current work with Shahn Majid at QMUL extends this into the framework of Quantum Riemannian Geometry, asking what a “quantum geodesic” means in a genuinely noncommutative setting, and whether the resulting geometry can shed new light on particle physics from first principles.

Emergent Gravity, Matrix Models & Algebraic Routes to Unification

The deepest and most speculative thread in my research concerns the question of whether spacetime, gravity, and ultimately the particle content of the universe can all emerge from a single, sufficiently rich algebraic structure—rather than being assumed at the outset. Two quite different approaches to this question have occupied me in recent years, and both point toward a common conviction: that the frontier of fundamental physics lies not in building ever larger particle colliders, but in finding the right mathematical language.

The first approach is through the IKKT (IIB) matrix model, a candidate non-perturbative formulation of string theory in which spacetime itself emerges as a configuration of matrices. In collaboration with Harold Steinacker at the University of Vienna, I studied the one-loop effective action for the geometry of 3+1-dimensional quantum branes within this model and derived modified Einstein equations governing their dynamics. These equations carry extra contributions from dilaton and axionic fields, as well as a novel “anharmonicity tensor” reflecting the classical Yang–Mills structure. Crucially, at cosmological scales the theory departs significantly from general relativity, yielding an asymptotically flat FLRW evolution and predicting extra geometric modes with features reminiscent of dark matter—a tantalising possibility that large-scale deviations from standard gravity might have a purely quantum geometric explanation.

The second approach draws on the remarkable mathematics of normed division algebras—the real numbers, complex numbers, quaternions, and octonions, the only four such algebras that exist. It has long been observed that the structure of the Standard Model fermions and gauge groups seems to fit with uncanny precision into these algebraic objects, particularly the octonions, whose eight-dimensional structure mirrors the eight quarks and leptons of a single generation. My postdoc with Nichol Furey at Humboldt University Berlin, and my ongoing project with Shahn Majid, explore how combining Furey’s division-algebraic approach with the Quantum Riemannian Geometry framework might illuminate the spectral geometry underpinning particle physics—asking whether the Standard Model is not merely consistent with these algebras but in some sense inevitable from them.

Affiliations

Mar, 2024 — ~Sep, 2027

School of Mathematical Sciences, Queen Mary University of London

I am currently working with Shahn Majid at QMUL Maths on an ambitious project funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG). The key idea is to understand the nature of quantum spacetime as per Beggs–Majid —e.g. what is a quantum geodesic?—and make use of this drastically new formulation to illuminate particle physics problems.

Jul, 2023 — Feb, 2024

Institute of Physics, Humboldt University Berlin

This short-term postdoc position at HU Berlin with my host Nichol Furey was really fruitful, generously funded by the host’s Freigeist grant from Volkswagen Stiftung. We worked on particle physics applications, combining Nichol’s unique approach to division-algebraic models with my expertise in non-commutative geometry à la Connes.

Summers 2023 & 2024

Erwin Schrödinger Institute, Vienna

These visits, funded by the JRF programme of ESI, led to a fruitful collaboration with Harold Steinacker at the Physics Department of the University of Vienna. We have a paper together on emergent gravity in the IKKT model, published in CQG.

Oct, 2018 — Jun, 2023

Institute for Theoretical Physics (LUH), Hannover

I worked with Olaf Lechtenfeld on various aspects of spacetime geometry in classical gauge theory, first as a doctoral scholar and later as a postdoc. This included works on de Sitter space for both Abelian (EM knots) and non-Abelian (cosmic gauge field) cases during the PhD, and on symmetric spaces as well as anti-de Sitter space during the postdoc.

2013 — 2018 (multiple short visits)

S.N. Bose National Centre for Basic Sciences, Kolkata

I visited the Bose Centre numerous times to collaborate with my favourite mentor Biswajit Chakraborty. A major portion of my research on Noncommutative quantum mechanics and Noncommutative geometry took place during three separate summer visits of over two months each, yielding three published articles.
